title: The Nuremberg indictment is filed
body:
The trial of the century did not begin in Nuremberg. It began with a stack of papers handed across a table in Berlin.

18 October 1945. In the Allied Control Authority Building, the new International Military Tribunal held its first session, with Soviet General Iona Nikitchenko presiding. Prosecutors for the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union each lodged a copy of the indictment.

It named 24 leading Nazis and charged them on four counts: conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. That last charge was new to international law.

The court then moved to Nuremberg, where the trial opened on 20 November 1945. Only 21 men sat in the dock. One had died before trial, one was ruled unfit, and Martin Bormann was tried in absentia.

sources.title: Minutes of the opening session, Avalon Project, Yale Law School
Indictment presented to the IMT, 18 October 1945, CVCE

threads:
The trial of the century did not start in Nuremberg. It started in Berlin.

18 October 1945. Prosecutors for the United States, Britain, France, and the Soviet Union lodged the indictment against 24 leading Nazis at the first session of the International Military Tribunal.

Four counts, including crimes against humanity, a charge new to international law. The trial opened in Nuremberg a month later.
photoCredit: The opening session of the International Military Tribunal in Berlin, 18 October 1945. Office of the U.S. Chief of Counsel, public domain.

declassified.fact: In Nuremberg, the job of handing the indictment to each prisoner fell to Major Airey Neave, a young British officer who had been the first Englishman to escape from Colditz Castle. When Neave served Hermann Göring, the former Reichsmarschall said only, "So it has come."

sources.title: The day of the indictment, Airey Neave, The Spectator (21 February 1976)
